Here are some best-practice tips for placing cameras so you can keep an eye on your Airbnb without overstepping guest privacy—always paired with full disclosure in your listing and in-home signage, and in compliance with local laws (especially around audio recording):

1. General Ground Rules  
   • Only monitor common areas (living room, kitchen, entryway, garage, exterior).   
   • Never install in private spaces (bedrooms, bathrooms, changing areas).   
   • Disclose every device and its location in your Airbnb listing and with a door-frame or welcome-book notice.  
   • Check local/state regulations—most jurisdictions require consent for any video or audio recording.

2. In-Plain-Sight—but Discreet—Mounts  
   • High Ceiling Corners: A small dome or bullet camera tucked up near the ceiling keeps it out of guests’ line of sight but still covers doorways and walkways.  
   • Above the Main Entrance: Over the door frame or porch soffit for exterior coverage—visible enough to deter break-ins, yet not front-and-center.  
   • Within a Smoke/CO Detector Housing: There are purpose-made housings that accept both a smoke detector and a mini camera. Guests see a detector, but the cam’s lens peers down the hall. (Verify that this complies with fire codes and local privacy laws.)

3. “Disguised” Everyday Objects  
   • Wall Clock or Picture Frame: Use a wall-mounted clock or picture frame whose lens peeks through a pin-hole in the décor. Keep the piece on a wall overlooking foot-traffic areas only.  
   • Faux Potted Plant or Bookshelf Décor: A small “spy cam” tucked in an artificial plant or among decorative books can survey the room without screaming “camera.”  
   • Wi-Fi Router / Cable Box Enclosures: If you have a shelf dedicated to electronics, some cameras are small enough to sit inconspicuously next to your router.

4. Technical Features to Protect Privacy  
   • Motion-Activated Recording: Cuts down on idle footage and keeps focus on genuine events.  
   • No Audio or One-Way Audio Only: In many areas audio recording without consent is illegal—consider disabling mics entirely.  
   • Privacy-Masking Zones: Many systems let you block out parts of the frame (e.g. kitchen counters or dining table) so that even in a common area you’re not capturing sensitive activity.

5. Operational Best Practices  
   • Focus on Entry/Exit Points & High-Traffic Spaces: These are the areas where you most need eyes-on coverage for security or emergencies.  
   • Keep Cameras at Least 7–8 Feet Above the Floor: Prevents guests from bumping them and reduces the chance of capturing intimate close-ups.  
   • Regularly Test & Update: Check angles, clean lenses, update firmware and passwords.  
   • Signage: A simple “This property is under 24-hour video surveillance” sign at the door goes a long way toward transparency and deterrence.

By following these guidelines you’ll have a low-profile security setup that watches the right spots without crossing into private areas—keeping both you and your guests safer and happier.
